name: Crest Whitestrips

angle.text: Users apply these strips over a one-to-three-week course to brighten their smile, and clinical trials report lightening of a shade or two. The change in tooth colour is visible and measurable, and it is one of the most widely used at-home whitening options.

summary: P&G's over-the-counter peroxide whitening strips; clinical trials show lightening of a shade or two, with sensitivity the usual trade-off.
note: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are commonly reported; results can fade.
currentQuick:
Crest Whitestrips are thin plastic strips coated with hydrogen peroxide gel that users stick to their teeth for a set time each day over one to three weeks. They launched in 2001 and are among the best-known at-home whitening products in the US.
Randomized trials exist, and general reviews describe strip systems as lightening teeth by around one or two shades.
How it works: The peroxide gel oxidises and breaks down stain-causing pigment molecules in and on the enamel, while the adhesive strip holds the gel against the tooth surface.
Risks and caveats: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects. They are not designed for crowns, veneers or fillings, and regulators differ on allowed peroxide strengths: the EU limits retail products to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.
deepLead:
Crest Whitestrips are over-the-counter teeth-whitening strips made by Procter & Gamble under the Crest brand. Thin flexible plastic strips coated with a peroxide gel are pressed onto the front surfaces of the teeth for a set period each day over a course of one to three weeks. They were announced in 2000 and launched to consumers in 2001.
The strips are used to lighten yellowing and surface staining from food, drinks, tobacco and ageing. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article describes strip systems generally as lightening teeth by about one or two shades, with results that vary by starting tooth colour and that can fade over time. Several randomized clinical trials of Crest Whitestrips have been published.
Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported side effects of peroxide whitening. Regulators treat peroxide strengths differently: the US FDA is described as endorsing gels below 6 percent hydrogen peroxide, while EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent.

name: Custom bleaching trays

angle.text: Dentist-fitted trays are used at home to lighten teeth with carbamide peroxide gel, and are a long-standing alternative to strips. The whitening is a visible change in tooth shade, and the method has been described in dental literature since the late 1980s.

summary: Dentist-fitted trays that hold carbamide peroxide gel against the teeth; the long-standing at-home alternative to strips.
note: Sensitivity is common; poorly fitting trays are linked to gum irritation.
currentQuick:
Custom bleaching trays are mouthpieces moulded to a person's teeth and filled with a peroxide gel, typically carbamide peroxide. They have been used since the late 1960s and are usually prescribed by a dentist.
Wikipedia describes tray bleaching as producing about one or two shades of lightening within days, with some fading afterwards.
How it works: The tray keeps the oxidising gel in contact with the teeth, where the peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in enamel and dentine.
Risks and caveats: Sensitivity is the most common side effect; gum irritation or burns are linked to high peroxide concentrations and ill-fitting trays. EU rules allow up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide only under dental supervision.
deepLead:
Custom bleaching trays are thin, fitted mouthpieces made from a mould of a person's teeth, loaded with a carbamide or hydrogen peroxide gel and worn for a set period at home, usually under dentist supervision. Wikipedia credits an orthodontist with introducing tray bleaching in the late 1960s, and notes that a 1989 paper by Haywood and Heymann supported the method.
Tray gels commonly use carbamide peroxide, which Wikipedia says was favoured because its effects were reported to last longer than hydrogen peroxide. Tray-based treatment is described as producing one or two shades of lightening within about three days, with worn times ranging from overnight to a few hours daily. Published clinical evidence in the available literature is limited to laboratory work on how trays and gel strength affect stain.

name: Whitening mouth rinse

angle.text: People use peroxide mouthwashes as a low-effort way to lighten tooth colour and reduce stain over weeks. Results are described as gradual, taking up to a few months, and the supporting evidence is mainly laboratory work.

summary: Peroxide mouthwash marketed for gradual stain lightening; the evidence base is mainly lab work and slow results are described.
note: Brief contact time; one case report of a gum burn after misuse.
currentQuick:
Whitening rinses are peroxide mouthwashes sold over the counter. Wikipedia describes use twice daily for a minute each, with visible results taking up to three months.
No clinical trials were found in the research behind this entry; most published work tests how rinses affect dental materials in the laboratory.
How it works: A peroxide in the rinse oxidises stain molecules, but contact with the teeth is short compared with strips or trays.
Risks and caveats: One case report documents a chemical gum burn after misuse. Peroxide at 10 percent or more is described as able to burn tissue, and EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.
deepLead:
Whitening mouth rinses are over-the-counter mouthwashes containing a peroxide intended to lighten tooth colour or reduce stain. Wikipedia lists rinses among at-home whitening methods, describing use twice daily for one minute each time, with visible results that can take up to three months.
Evidence available for this article consists mostly of laboratory studies, case reports and product analyses rather than clinical trials of cosmetic whitening.

name: Potassium nitrate desensitising toothpaste

chain: Whiter teeth over a full course
angle.text: Whitening users reach for this toothpaste to ease the sensitivity that often comes with peroxide bleaching, so they can complete a course and reach a brighter smile. It has been studied for dentine pain in general, not for whitening outcomes specifically.

summary: Ordinary desensitising toothpaste that whitening users reach for to calm sensitivity; studied for dentine pain, not for bleaching specifically.
note: Eases sensitivity at best; no evidence it permanently prevents whitening sensitivity.
currentQuick:
This is a toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, designed for dentine hypersensitivity. Whitening users sometimes use it because peroxide bleaching commonly causes tooth sensitivity.
Cochrane reviews examined potassium toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity; trials aimed specifically at whitening sensitivity were not found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: In vitro work has examined whether potassium nitrate occludes dentinal tubules.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia says such toothpastes can ease whitening sensitivity but there is no evidence of permanent prevention. It is an over-the-counter product.
deepLead:
Potassium nitrate desensitising toothpaste is a toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, a compound used to reduce dentine hypersensitivity, the sharp pain from exposed dentine in response to cold, heat or touch. In whitening communities it is mentioned as a product used around peroxide bleaching, because tooth sensitivity is the most common side effect of whitening.
Cochrane reviews have assessed potassium-containing toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article states that potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride toothpastes can ease whitening sensitivity, though there is no evidence they permanently prevent it.

name: Prophy paste polish

angle.text: Dental hygienists use this polishing paste to lift surface stain during a cleaning, leaving teeth looking cleaner and smoother. Appearance communities discuss it for stain removal; the research on it focuses on abrasivity and materials rather than cosmetic results.

summary: The gritty paste dental hygienists polish with; used for surface stain, with research focused on materials rather than cosmetic results.
note: Professional procedure; polishing pastes can alter composite surfaces in lab studies.
currentQuick:
Prophy paste is an abrasive polishing paste applied by a dental professional with a rubber cup during cleaning. It is used on surface stain and plaque rather than altering the tooth's inner colour.
Research located is mainly laboratory work on dental materials; no cosmetic trial of stain removal was found.
How it works: Fine abrasive particles in the paste are spun against the tooth to polish the surface and lift deposits.
Risks and caveats: Lab studies show polishing pastes can change roughness and gloss of composite resin restorations. It is a professional procedure.
deepLead:
Prophy paste is a gritty polishing paste applied with a rotating rubber cup, usually by a dental professional during a cleaning, to polish tooth surfaces and remove some surface deposits. It is relevant to appearance because it is used on extrinsic (surface) stain.
The available research examines the paste mostly in the laboratory, for its effects on restorative materials, porcelain and implant surfaces, rather than as a cosmetic whitening treatment in people.

name: Lip suction pump

angle.text: Users place the cup over the lips to make them look fuller, and the swelling is visible within minutes. The effect is temporary, and no studies of these devices were found.

summary: A vacuum cup that temporarily swells the lips; no studies found.
note: Effect described as temporary swelling; no research found.
currentQuick:
A lip suction pump is a vacuum device placed over the lips to make them look fuller for a short time.
No studies of it were found; only a brief description in an encyclopedia.
How it works: Wikipedia describes the vacuum as raising blood pressure in the lips, causing temporary swelling.
Risks and caveats: No risks specific to the device are documented in the sources found.
deepLead:
A lip suction pump is a hand-held vacuum device placed over the lips to make them look fuller. Wikipedia's lip plumper article describes such devices as using vacuum pumping to raise blood pressure in the lips, causing temporary swelling.
It is one of several non-injection plumping approaches, alongside topical plumpers whose irritant ingredients such as capsaicin cause swelling. Published information on the devices is sparse.

name: EarWell infant ear molding

chain: Ears of typical shape and position
angle.text: Parents and clinicians use this splinting system in the first weeks of life to reshape congenital ear differences such as lop or prominent ears without surgery. Clinical reports are consistently positive but lack controlled comparisons.

summary: A splint system that molds a newborn's malleable ear cartilage into shape in the first weeks of life, with consistent but uncontrolled clinical evidence behind it.
note: Studies report best results when started within the first weeks of life; most data come from retrospective or single-center series.
currentQuick:
EarWell is a non-surgical molding system placed on a newborn's ear to reshape cartilage deformities such as a folded or protruding ear. It is a pediatric medical device rather than an adult appearance product, and appears in this wiki as the non-surgical alternative to later ear surgery.
Published series from several centers, including in China and the United States, report that most treated ears improve when treatment starts early. No randomized controlled trial appears among the studies reviewed.
How it works: Researchers describe newborn ear cartilage as unusually pliable during the first weeks of life, attributed to circulating maternal estrogens [2][4]. A splint holds the ear in a corrected shape during this window so that the cartilage sets in the new form.
Risks and caveats: The reviewed studies describe treatment as non-invasive, with outcomes depending strongly on how early it begins and on deformity severity [4]. Skin irritation from adhesives is a general consideration for any taped device. Individual decisions are made with a pediatric or plastic-surgery clinician.
deepLead:
The EarWell Infant Ear Correction System is a non-surgical splinting system used to reshape congenital ear deformities in newborns, such as constricted (lop) ears, Stahl's ear and prominent ears. It is a molding approach in which a shaped device is adhered to the infant ear for a period of weeks .
Proponents among the plastic surgeons who developed and report on it say that the cartilage of a newborn is unusually plastic because of maternal estrogens, so molding begun in the first days or weeks of life can correct deformities that would otherwise be addressed by otoplasty later .
Published evidence consists mostly of single-center prospective and retrospective series, with correction rates generally reported as high when treatment starts early . No randomized controlled trial is listed among the studies reviewed here.

name: Dermastamp 0.5mm

angle.text: Forum users press this stamp onto skin and brows to boost topical absorption and soften fine lines, and some report it helps minoxidil on brows. Microneedling has been studied for skin texture and scars; the brow, eye-line and orbital-fat claims rest on anecdote.

summary: A handheld needle stamp used for microneedling; forum users apply it to brows, skin and to push topicals in, while the controlled evidence is thin.
note: Non-sterile or poorly handled needling carries infection risk; forum claims about fat loss or topical absorption are untested.
currentQuick:
A dermastamp is a small handheld device with short needles that is pressed vertically into skin, a form of microneedling. On looksmax.org it is discussed for eyebrows with minoxidil, for lines around the eyes and for skin texture.
Published work reviewed here is laboratory-style research on microneedle-assisted drug delivery, not trials of the stamp for appearance.
How it works: Microneedling punctures the skin repeatedly with tiny needles. Wikipedia describes it as a cosmetic procedure used for scarring and acne, and notes a pilot study of combining it with minoxidil for hair loss [1]. Forum users also say it helps topicals absorb [2].
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports a 2024 CDC report of three HIV diagnoses among patients of one New Mexico spa offering microneedling with platelet-rich plasma, attributed to infection-control concerns in non-medical settings [1].
deepLead:
A dermastamp is a handheld microneedling tool whose needle head is pressed straight down onto the skin, in contrast with a rolling dermaroller. A 0.5 mm needle length is a commonly discussed size in forum threads.
Microneedling in general is described as a cosmetic procedure that repeatedly punctures skin with tiny sterile needles, used for scarring and acne . A pilot study suggested combining it with minoxidil may treat hair loss better than minoxidil alone, according to Wikipedia .
On looksmax.org, users ask how often to use a stamp on brows alongside minoxidil, compare stamps with rollers, and discuss it for under-eye and laugh lines . No clinical trial of a 0.5 mm stamp specifically was found.

name: Red light mask (Omnilux/CurrentBody)

angle.text: Users wear these LED masks regularly in pursuit of fewer wrinkles, clearer skin and less puffiness. Red-light therapy has been studied for skin ageing and acne with mixed, often preliminary results, and consumer masks are less studied than clinical devices.

summary: Consumer LED face masks marketed for wrinkles and acne; the underlying red-light therapy has mixed, often preliminary evidence.
note: Evidence for the general technique is mixed; no mask-specific clinical studies were located for this entry.
currentQuick:
Red light masks are wearable LED devices that illuminate the face with red (and sometimes near-infrared or blue) light. Brands such as Omnilux and CurrentBody sell them for home use, marketed for skin quality.
The general approach, called LED light therapy or photobiomodulation, has been studied in dermatology with mixed and often preliminary results.
How it works: Encyclopedic descriptions say red and near-infrared light penetrate skin and act mainly on mitochondria, particularly cytochrome c oxidase, which proponents link to collagen production and reduced inflammation [1].
Risks and caveats: LED therapy is described as having fewer side effects than lasers; reported effects for low-level light include itching, red spots and mild allergic reactions, usually temporary [1].
deepLead:
A red light mask is a consumer LED device worn over the face that emits red light, sometimes combined with near-infrared or blue wavelengths, and is marketed for wrinkles, acne, puffiness and general skin appearance. Omnilux and CurrentBody are brand names associated with such masks.
The technique belongs to LED light therapy, in which low-level non-coherent light is intended to stimulate cellular repair through a process called photobiomodulation . Wikipedia describes research results as mixed and often preliminary .
No clinical trial of a specific Omnilux or CurrentBody mask was located for this article.

name: Photorejuvenation LED panel

chain: Red and near-infrared light on skin
angle.text: Users aim these home LED panels at the face or body for fine lines, texture, acne and hair growth. The mechanism is proposed from lab and clinical-device studies, while trials of consumer panels are limited.

summary: Home red/near-infrared LED panel sold for skin rejuvenation; the mechanism is proposed and consumer-panel evidence is thin.
note: Evidence summarised here comes from LED therapy in general, not tested consumer panels.
currentQuick:
A photorejuvenation LED panel is a home light array, typically red and near-infrared, used on the face for skin appearance.
Supporters cite studies of LED therapy in dermatology. The summary available for this entry gives no effect sizes and does not compare home panels with clinical devices.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is photobiomodulation: light absorbed by mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase, thought to increase ATP production and nitric oxide release. This pathway is described as suggested rather than settled.
Risks and caveats: Photobiomodulation is generally described as safe, with infrequent transient itching, red spots or mild allergic reactions. Regulatory status of consumer panels was not established in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
A photorejuvenation LED panel is a flat array of light-emitting diodes, usually emitting red and near-infrared light, that users hold or mount near the face or body at home. Marketing and user discussion associate such panels with skin rejuvenation, including fine lines, texture and acne, and with hair growth.
The underlying technique is called photobiomodulation. Wikipedia describes it as low-level light applied without a photosensitising agent, with the proposed target being cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria, a mechanism the article presents as suggested rather than settled. Red and near-infrared wavelengths (roughly 600 to 1000 nm) penetrate tissue more deeply than blue or green light.
The Wikipedia summary reports studies of red-light LED therapy for collagen enhancement, acne, rosacea and hair loss, but gives no effect sizes or sample sizes, and it does not evaluate how consumer panels compare with clinical equipment.

name: Ultrasound scaler (home)

angle.text: Appearance communities discuss home scalers as a way to remove visible tartar and stain between dental visits. Research covers professional ultrasonic scalers; home units have not been studied the same way.

summary: Consumer version of the dental ultrasonic scaler for tartar removal; research covers professional devices, not home units.
note: Research on enamel and root effects concerns professional use.
currentQuick:
A home ultrasonic scaler is a consumer tool modelled on the instrument dental hygienists use to remove tartar and stain.
Published work studies professional devices. No studies of home-use scalers were found.
How it works: Professional scalers vibrate at high frequency, loosen deposits and flush debris with a liquid spray.
Risks and caveats: Professional-setting research reports aerosol and splatter generation, and notes possible damage to enamel, restorations and root surfaces. Home-use safety data were not found.
deepLead:
A home ultrasonic scaler is a consumer version of the vibrating instrument that dental professionals use to remove calculus (tartar), plaque and stain from teeth. Users in appearance communities discuss it as a way to remove tartar at home.
Published research on ultrasonic scaling concerns professional devices. Wikipedia describes them as electric tools that vibrate at high frequency and use a water spray to cool the tip and flush debris, and notes that research differs on whether they match hand instruments in effectiveness. No studies of home-use scalers were found.

name: 1-Testosterone (1-Test / dihydroboldenone)

angle.text: Sold online as a prohormone supplement, it was used by bodybuilders seeking muscle size and a bigger physique. It has been a controlled substance in the US since 2005, and there are no human trials of its effects.

summary: A DHT-derived designer steroid once sold online as a supplement; controlled in the US since 2005 and untested in human trials.
note: Controlled substance in the US; animal data only.
currentQuick:
1-Testosterone is a synthetic androgen sold in the past as a muscle-building prohormone.
Only animal data and doping-detection literature are described; no human trials were found.
How it works: It binds the androgen receptor selectively, and an animal study reported potency comparable to testosterone propionate in androgen-sensitive tissues.
Risks and caveats: In the animal study it also increased liver weight. It has been a US Schedule III substance since 2005.
deepLead:
1-Testosterone (1-Test, 1-T, dihydroboldenone) is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 5-alpha-reduced derivative of boldenone, differing from testosterone by a double bond at the 1(2) position. It has been sold as a supplement or prohormone for muscle building.
According to Wikipedia, it was legally sold online in the United States until 2005, when it became a Schedule III controlled substance. No clinical trials of 1-testosterone were found.

name: Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T)

angle.text: An oral designer androgen sold in early-2000s supplements aimed at bodybuilders chasing muscle size. Evidence for the muscle-building use is anecdotal, with animal work and a kidney-injury case report as the main published material.

summary: An oral designer androgen once sold as a prohormone supplement; known from animal work and a kidney-injury case report.
note: Prohibited in sport; case report of kidney injury with ciclosporin.
currentQuick:
M1T is an oral anabolic steroid that appeared in bodybuilding supplements in the 2000s without medical approval.
Research is limited to animal and in vitro work, analytical papers and a case report.
How it works: It is an androgen receptor agonist; a 2011 study tested receptor affinity and anabolic and androgenic potency in animals.
Risks and caveats: A case report describes acute kidney injury after combining it with ciclosporin. It is on the WADA prohibited list.
deepLead:
Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T, SC-11195) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of 1-testosterone. It was never marketed for medical use. It appeared in the early 2000s in over-the-counter supplements aimed at bodybuilders.
A 2011 study identified M1T in a supplement and examined it in animal and in vitro models; a published case report links it to kidney injury through an interaction with ciclosporin. The World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as prohibited.

name: Methylstenbolone (M-Sten / Hybrid)

angle.text: Sold online as a supplement or research chemical, it is used by lifters seeking muscle gain and a harder physique. It has never been trialled in people; published human material is a case report of cholestatic jaundice.

summary: An oral designer androgen sold as a supplement or research chemical; no trials, with a case report of cholestatic jaundice.
note: Prohibited in sport; liver injury case report.
currentQuick:
Methylstenbolone is an unapproved oral androgen sold online in muscle-building supplements.
Research is mostly about detecting and metabolising it, plus a few case reports.
How it works: It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist; 17-alpha methylation is associated with oral activity.
Risks and caveats: A case report links a product containing it to cholestatic jaundice. It is prohibited in sport and has no approved medical use.
deepLead:
Methylstenbolone (M-Sten, Methyl-Sten, Ultradrol) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 17-alpha-methylated derivative of stenbolone. It was never introduced for medical use and has been sold online as a nutritional supplement.
Published work consists mainly of metabolism and doping-detection studies, supplement analyses and a case report of cholestatic jaundice.

name: Methyldienolone (Methyldienolone / M-Dien)

angle.text: An unmarketed oral 19-nor androgen that appears in bodybuilding discussion as a muscle-building compound. Almost nothing is published beyond detection chemistry, so its muscle effect in people is untested.

summary: An unmarketed oral 19-nor androgen; almost nothing published beyond detection chemistry.
note: Prohibited in sport; no human data found.
currentQuick:
Methyldienolone is an oral 19-nortestosterone derivative that was never marketed as a drug.
The literature consists of chemistry and doping-control papers.
How it works: It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist; no pharmacokinetic detail was found.
Risks and caveats: No adverse-effect data were found. It is prohibited in sport and listed as Schedule III in the US per Wikipedia.
deepLead:
Methyldienolone (RU-3467) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, a 17-alpha-methylated 19-nortestosterone derivative. It has not been marketed as a medicine. Published literature is sparse.
Wikipedia lists it as a US Schedule III substance and as prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.

name: Dimethyltrienolone (Dimethyltren / RU-2420)

angle.text: A never-marketed trenbolone analog that comes up in bodybuilding circles for its reported animal potency, said to be far above methyltestosterone. No human data exist, so its muscle-building use is speculative.

summary: An obscure, never-marketed trenbolone analog with reported animal potency far above methyltestosterone and no human data.
note: No human studies exist; described as likely severely hepatotoxic. Not approved anywhere.
currentQuick:
Dimethyltrienolone is an experimental oral anabolic steroid made in the 1960s by Roussel Uclaf. It was never sold as a medicine and has not been tested in people.
In animal assays it was reported as extremely potent, and some commentators call it one of the strongest steroids ever made. All of that rests on rodent and receptor-binding work.
How it works: It activates the androgen and progesterone receptors strongly and, like trenbolone, is not converted by aromatase or 5α-reductase. Methyl groups at two positions make it resistant to liver breakdown, allowing oral activity.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data exist. Reference sources describe it as expected to be highly liver-toxic and note progestogenic effects. It has no approved medical use and is available only as an unregulated research chemical.
deepLead:
Dimethyltrienolone, developmental code RU-2420 and also written 7α,17α-dimethyltrenbolone, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS). It is a 17α-alkylated derivative of the 19-nortestosterone family that includes nandrolone, trenbolone and metribolone .
It was first described in 1967 and has never been marketed for medical use . Reference works describe it as an extremely potent agonist of the androgen and progesterone receptors, with animal bioassays reporting more than 100 times the anabolic and androgenic potency of methyltestosterone . It has been called "perhaps the most potent" AAS developed, a characterisation that Wikipedia attributes to a secondary source rather than to human data .
No human clinical, pharmacokinetic or safety studies have been published. Its liver toxicity is described as likely to be severe on structural grounds, but this too is inferred from related compounds rather than measured in people . It circulates in bodybuilding circles only as an unapproved research chemical.

name: Metribolone (R1881 / Methyltrienolone)

angle.text: Best known as a laboratory standard for androgen receptor studies, it was dropped as a drug and appears in doping cases and underground muscle-building talk. Its use for physique goals is based on anecdote rather than trials.

summary: A lab-standard androgen receptor ligand that was dropped as a drug for liver toxicity and shows up in doping cases.
note: Abandoned clinically over severe liver toxicity; WADA-banned; never approved.
currentQuick:
Metribolone is an oral anabolic steroid made from trenbolone in the 1960s. It was tried for advanced breast cancer but dropped because it damaged the liver at very low doses.
Today it is mainly a research reagent for studying the androgen receptor, though it has also turned up in doping tests and in bodybuilding circles.
How it works: It binds the androgen receptor very tightly and resists breakdown by 5α-reductase and aromatase. It also binds the progesterone receptor and, more weakly, other steroid receptors.
Risks and caveats: Documented effects include liver toxicity and virilisation. It has no approved use, is banned in sport, and has no controlled modern human studies.
deepLead:
Metribolone, also called methyltrienolone and by the code R1881, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) and the 17α-methyl derivative of trenbolone . It has never been approved for medical use.
It was tested clinically in the late 1960s and early 1970s as a possible treatment for advanced breast cancer in women, but development ended because of liver toxicity at very low doses . Since the mid-1970s it has been a standard tool in laboratories, where radiolabelled R1881 is used as a high-affinity ligand to measure androgen receptor binding .
Outside the lab, metribolone has appeared in sports doping and bodybuilding. Reference sources describe it as among the most potent and most liver-toxic AAS; in rats it was reported at 120 to 300 times the oral anabolic potency of methyltestosterone, though Wikipedia notes that comparable potency has not been seen in humans .

name: Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG / The Clear)

angle.text: The 2003 designer steroid made to evade doping tests, taken by athletes for muscle and performance. It is potent in laboratory assays and has never been studied in people.

summary: The 2003 "designer steroid" built to slip past doping tests; potent in lab work, never studied in people.
note: Schedule III in the US; never approved or safety-tested; tied to the BALCO scandal.
currentQuick:
THG is a steroid made by modifying gestrinone so that doping labs would not recognise it. It surfaced in 2003 when a used syringe was handed to anti-doping officials, and it became the centrepiece of the BALCO scandal.
It is mostly known from doping history and detection research rather than from appearance or bodybuilding use.
How it works: It binds the androgen receptor about as tightly as DHT, also activates progesterone receptors, and binds the glucocorticoid receptor. Rat studies showed it promotes muscle growth.
Risks and caveats: It has never been tested in clinical trials, so its effects in people are uncharacterised; infertility, acne and hirsutism are listed with prolonged use. It is a US Schedule III substance and banned in sport.
deepLead:
Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), nicknamed "The Clear", is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid made by chemically modifying the gynecological drug gestrinone. It was never approved for medical use .
It became known in 2003 as the first prominent "designer steroid": a compound built so that existing doping tests would not detect it. A spent syringe containing it was passed to the US Anti-Doping Agency, and Don Catlin's UCLA laboratory identified it by mass spectrometry; the findings were published in 2004 . The episode was central to the BALCO scandal, which involved sprinters and baseball players .
Laboratory studies show THG binds strongly to the androgen receptor and also to progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors, and it promoted muscle growth in rats . No human clinical safety or efficacy trials exist.

name: Desoxymethyltestosterone (DMT / Madol)

angle.text: A 1960s oral steroid revived as a designer doping agent and supplement ingredient for muscle gain. The evidence is limited to animal data, with no human trials of the physique use.

summary: A 1960s oral steroid revived in 2005 as a designer doping agent and supplement ingredient; animal data only.
note: US Schedule III; WADA-banned; products sold under its name have been mislabelled.
currentQuick:
Desoxymethyltestosterone is an oral anabolic steroid invented in 1961 and shelved. It resurfaced in 2005 when it was supplied to the BALCO operation and was later found in bodybuilding supplements.
All evidence about its effects comes from rat and cell studies; there are no clinical trials.
How it works: It is a modified form of DHT that activates the androgen receptor and increased muscle mass in castrated rats with little effect on prostate weight.
Risks and caveats: Animal studies at higher doses reported liver damage and heart enlargement. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, Class C in the UK, and prohibited in sport. Supplements labelled with it have sometimes contained other compounds.
deepLead:
Desoxymethyltestosterone (DMT, also called Madol and sold under names such as Pheraplex) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, a 17α-methyl derivative of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) that lacks the usual 3-keto group . It is unrelated to the hallucinogen dimethyltryptamine, which shares the abbreviation .
It was invented by Max Huffman in 1961 and described in 1963, but never marketed as a drug . It re-emerged in 2005, when chemist Patrick Arnold produced it and supplied it to Victor Conte of BALCO; it was identified as a doping agent and found in over-the-counter bodybuilding supplements .
Rat studies indicate substantial anabolic activity, and in vitro tests found it activates the androgen receptor; no clinical trials of it exist . It is a US Schedule III controlled substance and prohibited in sport .

name: Prostanozol

angle.text: A designer prohormone sold in bodybuilding supplements to deliver a stanozolol-like effect for lean muscle. It is now a Schedule III substance in the US and has no clinical data.

summary: A designer prohormone steroid once sold in bodybuilding supplements; now a Schedule III substance with no clinical data.
note: US Schedule III since 2012; WADA-banned; no human trials.
currentQuick:
Prostanozol is a designer steroid that was sold in bodybuilding supplements from around 2005. It is chemically a prodrug of a stanozolol-like compound.
It has no clinical trials behind it; what is published concerns doping detection and legal classification.
How it works: It is described as being converted in the body to a stanozolol analogue lacking the 17α-methyl group and acting as an androgen receptor agonist.
Risks and caveats: Human safety has not been studied. It is a US Schedule III substance and prohibited in sport, and a 2007 marathon runner was banned after testing positive.

Prostanozol, also called demethylstanozolol tetrahydropyran ether, is a designer anabolic-androgenic steroid that acts as a prodrug of the 17α-demethylated analogue of stanozolol (Winstrol) . It is taken by mouth .
It was first identified in 2005 as an ingredient in products sold as bodybuilding "dietary supplements" . In 2007 Russian marathon runner Lyubov Denisova tested positive for prostanozol and testosterone and received a two-year ban . In 2012 the US Drug Enforcement Administration classified it, along with methasterone, as a Schedule III anabolic steroid .
Published work is limited to doping-control metabolism studies and supplement-contamination surveys; there are no clinical trials .
